1089dcf7-ccf9-5327-a627-5d187eeff616.title: Seasonal Cuisine
1089dcf7-ccf9-5327-a627-5d187eeff616.quote: While the shifting lunar calendar determined the timing of religious festivities, it was the seasons of the solar calendar that defined the flavours on the table.

1929cd0e-6d83-5217-b6f4-6dafbb13c89b.title: Environment
1929cd0e-6d83-5217-b6f4-6dafbb13c89b.presentation:
Over the centuries Islamic civilisation developed sustainable farming methods that balanced care for the environment with human needs. By securing reliable water supplies a variety of crops could be grown and harvested several times a year. Farmers used organic fertilisers and rotated crops to keep the soil fertile and avoid overuse. Water management and erosion control showed their dedication to protecting natural resources.  
  
Muslim scholars built on knowledge from Greek and Roman authors such as Theophrastus and Columella, improving techniques in farming and irrigation. Books by Ibn al-Awwam and Ibn Bassal offered advice on soil care, cultivation, and water use, ensuring these methods stayed effective over time. These agricultural innovations also shaped culinary traditions.  
  
Despite its origins in a single faith, the cuisine reflected a blend of diverse cultures enriched through ongoing exchanges. While changing seasons influenced the range of available ingredients, religious festivities frequently encouraged more elaborate meals.  
  
Different cooking vessels were created from various materials to enhance the flavours of ingredients. The design of serving dishes reflected the artistic tastes of communities, revealing social structure and the shared experience of dining. These connections between farming, food, and culture highlight the creativity and sustainability of Islamic traditions.

197de4dc-e60d-526d-91ef-7ab61f66baca.title: Interfaith Hospitality
197de4dc-e60d-526d-91ef-7ab61f66baca.quote: Shelter and food to all comers.

238a4c4f-8bb3-584d-829b-208cef78fb0c.title: Social Life
238a4c4f-8bb3-584d-829b-208cef78fb0c.presentation:
Throughout history, food has played a central role in religious practices, serving as a medium for feasts and sacrifices that connect individuals to the divine. These communal meals become a medium to express shared beliefs and social hierarchies. As such, food acts as a powerful language that defines religions and, by extension, societies. The rituals and traditions around the table turn eating into an act of connection and create moments of intimacy and belonging.  
  
In Islamic culture, certain foods, such as dates and coffee, hold profound religious and cultural significance. These foods embody values and traditions deeply rooted in the faith, symbolising gratitude, greeting, and divine provision. The symbolic meaning of food extends to the act of sharing, encapsulated in the expression "*khubz wa meleh"*" (bread and salt), which signifies trust and the bonds forged through communal eating.  
  
Food also acts as a social bond in creating a common identity with generosity and charity at its heart. The Qur'an emphasises feeding those in need, turning the simple act of offering a meal into an expression of compassion and care that transcends the different landscapes of the Islamic world. From bustling urban gatherings inside the city walls to the warm, welcoming embrace in a Bedouin tent, food becomes a language of belonging and solidarity.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1.title: Food Sharing as an Intimate Ritual
2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1.quote: Sharing a meal goes beyond its physical meaning, it transcends into creating a social bond with guests, families and even lovers, creating an intimate bond captured in the Arabic concept of خبز وملح or “bread and salt“.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877.title: Palatial Plates: Dishes and Diets of Islamic Courts
2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877.quote: Islamic court cuisine featured a wide variety of dishes. Regions like Egypt excelled in culinary artistry, while Ottoman expansion introduced new dishes like vegetable stews and honey-infused desserts. Diets at the sultan’s table were often guided by court physicians, incorporating herbs and medicinal ingredients to ensure health and balance.

340e2c5d-de63-5f2d-aff1-0202018fb322.title: Gender Roles in Food Production and Preparation
340e2c5d-de63-5f2d-aff1-0202018fb322.quote: In the Islamic world, food preparation highlighted social hierarchies and gender roles. Women played key roles in cooking, from milling grains to baking bread, while elite homes employed skilled cooks. Middle-class families relied on communal ovens, and public kitchens funded by the wealthy served soldiers and the poor, making food central to both daily life and cultural identity.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902.title: Food Nomadism: from the Desert Tradition to the Urban Table
39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902.quote: Between the traditional rural and urban environments, the act of sharing food in gatherings highlights different cultural milieus. These traditions changed with the urbanisation of Muslim communities leaving the desert and embarking on city life.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c.title: Etiquette: The Protocol of Sitting at the Table with the Sultan
44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c.quote: Dining in Islamic courts adhered to strict protocols that reflected social hierarchy and decorum. Historical sources describe the sultan seated at the head of a table in the throne hall, flanked by princes according to their ranks. Tables varied in shape – long or round – and were supervised by officials like the *saqi*, a private cupbearer who served drinks. Food safety was a paramount, with tasters and gemstone vessels believed to detect poison used to protect the sultan.

4820bede-ded6-5414-b6ec-aadb0f259f5a.title: Gender Roles in Agriculture, Animal Husbandry, and the Food Industry
4820bede-ded6-5414-b6ec-aadb0f259f5a.quote: Men and women in the Islamic world shared roles in agriculture, animal husbandry and the food industry. Women cultivated crops, managed livestock, traded goods and owned properties like orchards and grain silos. Men focused on large-scale trade and specialised professions. Together, their contributions sustained rural and urban economies, with food production reflecting a balance of shared and distinct responsibilities essential to society.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e.title: Food Symbolism in Islamic Culture
6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e.quote: In Islamic culture, certain types of food hold profound significance beyond physical nourishment, serving spiritual and cultural purposes. These foods embody cultural identity, religious rituals and a deeper sense of gratitude for divine provisions.

6cb087a8-0f2b-5d20-968d-ab61f692867d.title: The Diversity of the Tableware
6cb087a8-0f2b-5d20-968d-ab61f692867d.quote: They explored how heat interacts with the natural qualities of food in clay, metal, or stoneware vessels, achieving the perfect combination of flavors to be served on plates that enhance the visual appeal of the dish.

735e5e35-f62a-5302-96aa-f2e9a69130dd.title: Gendered Roles
735e5e35-f62a-5302-96aa-f2e9a69130dd.presentation:
Gender roles in food production and preparation in the Islamic world reflect a dynamic balance of responsibilities. Women were central to agriculture, cultivating crops, managing livestock and processing goods for trade. They owned agricultural properties, including date plantations and grain silos, and sold products like oil, eggs and poultry in markets, showcasing their autonomy. Men often handled labour-intensive tasks such as ploughing fields, irrigation and transporting goods. In cities, male butchers, bakers and street cooks dominated food professions, preparing and selling meats, bread and confections.  
  
Food preparation varied across social classes. Elite households employed both male and female servants, with women supervising kitchens in the *haramlek*. Female slave cooks during the Fatimid and Ayyubid periods were renowned for their expertise. Middle-class households relied on communal ovens, while public kitchens, funded by both men and women elites through *waqf* endowments, provided food to soldiers, students and the poor, symbolising charity and religious devotion. Women played a key role in sustaining these kitchens and ensuring communal welfare.  
  
Banquets highlighted social status and power. Male officers like the *saqi* (cupbearer) managed food service, ensuring drinks were properly prepared and served, while women in the *haramlek* prepared elaborate dishes. Female musicians, singers and dancers elevated courtly gatherings with their performances, enhancing cultural refinement.  
  
The collaboration between men and women in food production, trade and presentation reveals a shared responsibility in shaping the culinary and social legacy of the Islamic world.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340.title: Culinary Syncretism
8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340.quote: “A cup of coffee commits one to forty years of friendship”. A Turkish proverb

88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3.title: Food Rules and Recommendations
88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3.quote: “He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, pig’s meat, and animals over which any name other than God’s has been invoked. But if anyone is forced to eat such things by hunger, rather than desire or excess, he commits no sin: God is most merciful and forgiving” (2:173/Al-Baqara).

91c22cc7-61aa-5122-9cb0-9b4edc616779.title: Professional Roles in Food Preparation and Table Service
91c22cc7-61aa-5122-9cb0-9b4edc616779.quote: In the Islamic world, food preparation professions ranged from skilled female cooks and saqis serving courts to male-dominated street markets with bakers, butchers and vendors. Female slaves excelled as cooks in elite households, while the saqi symbolised grace and service, blending functionality and artistry in culinary roles across social and cultural settings.

99437e6b-b376-5f86-9a58-f2f1bbf55c32.title: Religion
99437e6b-b376-5f86-9a58-f2f1bbf55c32.presentation:
Theme III explores ways in which Islamic religious beliefs have shaped food practices in daily life, and examines religious guidance about what is permissible to eat, how food should be prepared, and the etiquette of sharing meals. Food traditions of Ramadan and the Eids, and the importance of the kitchen in certain Sufi spiritual training practices are also addressed.  
  
Food and faith in Islamic culture are closely entwined. Culinary practices encompass not only food preparation, but are expressions of spirituality, community, and ethics. This Theme looks at dietary laws, celebrations, and spiritual education, inviting viewers to explore the historical and religious aspects of food across the Islamic world. Visitors may gain a deeper understanding of how food nurtures both body and soul, and can reinforce a connection to the divine.

b7ef5340-5385-5a3c-a441-d738e99f2269.title: Coexistence
b7ef5340-5385-5a3c-a441-d738e99f2269.presentation:
From the birth of Islam, many laws and frameworks were established to regulate daily interactions among communities of different religions. These measures laid the foundation for periods of coexistence, which varied in degree depending on the time, place, and political regime.  
  
While religious differences sometimes posed challenges that required careful management, they also fostered rich cultural exchanges. Beyond religious distinctions, cultures often influenced one another profoundly, creating interconnected worlds where ideas, art, and traditions were shared. Food, as a strong social and identity marker, was no exception. It played and is still playing a pivotal role in both the cohesion and differentiation of these multicultural environments.  
  
This theme explores food as a social mediator, examining the practice of hospitality in which meals brought people together and facilitated connections. It highlights how interactions among interfaith communities, cultures, and traditions gave rise to thriving food industries, rich material cultures, and continuous culinary innovations.  
  
Across the Islamic world, food united people more than it divided them, fostering connections that transcended differences.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c.title: Feasts
bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c.quote: Feasts were a central feature of courtly life, held daily and divided into private and public gatherings. Records from the Mamluk era describe elaborate celebrations, with up to five feasts a day and special events like weddings or circumcision ceremonies lasting several days. One grand circumcision feast reportedly continued for 40 days, showcasing the court’s opulence and capacity for large-scale hospitality.

c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8.title: The Balance Between Food and Nature
c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8.quote: As Islam expanded, a profound agricultural transformation began to take shape. By the AH 5th / 11th century it had spread from Spain to Transoxiana, reshaping production, livelihoods, urban centres, and daily life.

cacd508c-ac3e-57b1-bbbe-26babcbf2131.title: Kitchen as a Medium of Education in Islam
cacd508c-ac3e-57b1-bbbe-26babcbf2131.quote: “I was raw, I was cooked, I was burned” Mevlana/ Divan-ı Kebir.

d5ad3026-c4d4-5745-afb9-164c36e226b9.title: Men and Women Preparing a Table
d5ad3026-c4d4-5745-afb9-164c36e226b9.quote: Banquets in the Islamic world reflected social hierarchy and gender roles. Women often prepared meals or worked in the haramlek, while male servants attended men. Gender-segregated dining was common, and grand events featured shared dishes, luxury vessels and entertainment by musicians and dancers, showcasing the cultural and social significance of communal feasting.

d6e87885-c723-578b-94ce-90f46d8638c0.title: About
d6e87885-c723-578b-94ce-90f46d8638c0.presentation:
This exhibition by Museum With No Frontiers explores the Islamic world through its rich culinary traditions. It aims to deepen understanding of Islamic culture and promote cross-cultural dialogue. What sets this exhibition apart is its unique international team of individuals from different cultures and backgrounds, a microcosm of the Museum With No Frontiers’ culturally diverse contributors.  
  
Food is a basic human necessity that can unite or divide, foster peace, or spark conflict. It is not merely a means of survival, but a reflection of cultural identity, personal preferences, and the dynamics of social, political, and economic power.  
  
In regions where heritage threatened, highlighting the culinary traditions of the Islamic world reinforces cultural pride and resilience. It provides a platform to foster tolerance by illustrating how foods transcend borders, reflect shared histories and encourage coexistence.  
  
In today’s globalised world, food culture serves as an ambassador, capable of wielding soft power to bridge divides. This exhibition celebrates food’s universal language, emphasising its role in shaping identities, preserving heritages and promoting understanding across cultures.

d895a076-21e8-5cd0-809f-8d8046a05a60.title: Food at Islamic Courts
d895a076-21e8-5cd0-809f-8d8046a05a60.presentation:
During the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, from the 8th to the 13th centuries (AH 2nd to 7th centuries), various kinds of foods became popular, such as grilled kebabs, meat pies, soups, and fruit juices. These were central to the cuisine of the time, and reflect the varied culinary heritage of the Islamic world.  
  
The sultan’s kitchens prepared food not only for the sultan himself, but also for the many inhabitants of the citadel. Historical accounts describe the sultan’s kitchen as having an “inextinguishable fire,” referring to its continuous operation to meet the demands of daily banquets and special celebrations. These banquets were held regularly, for marriages, circumcision ceremonies, sports events, or the dispatching of the *mahmal* (a ceremonial pilgrimage procession).  
  
The Islamic court was familiar with dining tables (*sufra*) long or round. Historical records tell us that the sultan dined in grand halls like the Hall of Columns or of *iwan*. The sultan would sit at the head of the table, with princes and other dignitaries seated to his right and left according to their ranks.  
  
The Ottoman caliphate, which expanded around the Mediterranean from Serbia to North Africa, introduced new culinary traditions to the western Islamic world. These included stuffed vegetables, yogurt-based dishes, rice, and sweet pastries filled with nuts and dipped in honey or syrup. The Mughal empire in India combined the spicy flavours of curry with influences from Iranian and Central Asian cuisines. In the Mughal palace of Emperor Akbar food was often prepared with chilies and served with an array of diverse ingredients.  
  
The importance of food in the Islamic world is also reflected in the craftsmanship of its dinnerware. Bowls, pitchers, cups, spoons, and large plates were often intricately designed, underscoring the cultural and social significance of food in Islamic society.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515.title: Religious Festivals, Preparation and Dishes
d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515.quote: "The day of Arafah, the day of sacrifice, the days of tashriq are (the days of) our festival, O people of Islam. These are the days of eating and drinking" (Sunan Abi Dawud, 2419).

ee52ce40-15e6-5226-940a-be419a8f8606.title: Preservation Methods and Innovation
ee52ce40-15e6-5226-940a-be419a8f8606.quote: In Islamic culture preservation techniques like drying, salting, and pickling in vinegar or brine ensured food stability, while innovations like crystallising fruits and cold storage supported culinary diversity and sustainability across regions.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782.title: Food as a Bond of Communal Identity
efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782.quote: “… and give food—despite their desire for it—to the poor, the orphan, and the captive.” (Al-Insan 5 - 8). In the Islamic culture, sharing food with people in need is a blessing and a social and charitable act.

f409fb59-4b8b-5176-b415-788d1bc965d4.title: Duties and Roles of Court Officers Serving Rulers and Nobility
f409fb59-4b8b-5176-b415-788d1bc965d4.quote: At Islamic courts, food and dining rituals reflected power and hierarchy, with officers like the Amir-shikar managing hunting feasts and the saqi symbolising elite service. Grand banquets reinforced authority, while specific roles ensured order and tradition. Gendered and hierarchical roles in court dining showcased the interplay of culture, politics and social status.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32.title: Food-related Craftsmanship and Industries from and for the Islamic World
fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32.quote: When people of diverse faiths and traditions come together, they do not merely share their knowledge; they blend their arts, crafts, and ways of life into a tapestry that reflects the richness of humanity.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/194.contextual_description:
In the painting, a young prince sits on a carpet outdoors, respectfully extending his hands toward a holy man who gestures to share wisdom. A nearby sapling adds a natural touch.  
  
To the left of the holy man is his attendant with a book, while another attendant on the prince’s right holds his belongings. In the foreground, a musician plays a sitar with a dog behind him, and a servant stands by a small table with a vase, dish, fresh fruit and a red box.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/7a3.contextual_description:
This miniature is the right page of a bifolium depicting a *majlis* hosted by Selim II (r. AH 974-982/1566-1574), who was most probably still Prince at the moment of this portrait.  
  
*Majalis* were engaging formal assembly where discussion, music, poetry, food, drinks and etiquettes shaped courtly rituals. The structured hierarchy between the attendees is evident as boon companions, courtiers, servants, and musicians face with deference a striking representation of Prince Selim (on the left folio), adhering to strict ceremonial decorum and following appropriate protocol when attending such courtly event.  
  
The presence of attendants serving drinks and musicians highlight the importance of hospitality and the leisurely atmosphere of the AH 10th / AD 16th century Ottoman court.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/a2c.contextual_description:
This miniature is the left page of a bifolium depicting a *majlis* hosted by Selim II (r. AH 974-982/1566-1574), who was most probably still Prince at the moment of this portraiture. *Majalis* were important engaging assembly where discussions, music, poetry, food, drink, and etiquette shaped courtly rituals.  
  
Prince Selim, looking towards his guests and servants represented on the right folio, is depicted larger than life in a royal kiosk holding delicately a cup of wine in his right hand while grabbing firmly a handkerchief, symbol of sovereignty, in his left hand. His impressive stature, conventional cross-legged position and the lavishness of his clothes accentuate this vivid expression of power.  
  
The depiction of dining, entertainment, and formal conduct in Ottoman court culture underscores the importance of etiquette and ceremonial feasting within this cultural context.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/54a.contextual_description:
The manuscript *Divan-i Shahi* is a collection of poems by Amir Shahi Sabzavari, reflecting the cultural and social atmosphere of his time, often featuring feasts and celebrations.  
  
On the back of the binding, a courtly celebration is depicted, with a ruler, likely Sultan Selim I, on a golden throne surrounded by members of his court in an outdoor setting. Courtiers converse while servants serve refreshments. Amir Shahi's poetry frequently mentions royal banquets and celebratory events, enriched by imagery of wine, music, and companionship that embody courtly life.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/cdc.contextual_description:
This version of *Iyar-i Danish*, created for Emperor Akbar (1556–1605) at the Mughal court, is noteworthy for its “mirrors for princes” genre, teaching rulers effective governance through moral tales. Each chapter contains a frame narrative that illustrates a specific moral through the characters’ stories.  
  
Mughal Emperor Akbar’s court showcased a grand, cosmopolitan culture, reflecting influences from Persian, Central Asian, Indian and Middle Eastern traditions, particularly in its culinary and social practices.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/110.contextual_description: A large brass tray with extensive silver inlay. The layout is a study in circles: the central motif, a geometric pattern itself derived from intersecting circles, is linked to three circles which divide the surrounding inscription into equal parts. The whole composition serves as a framework for no less than seven inscriptions, whose verticals, arranged like spokes within wheels, provide a striking and satisfying visual contrast. The largest inscription reads, “Glory to our master the sultan, the wise, the diligent, the just, the warlike king – may his victory be glorified”!

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/beb.contextual_description: This large, elaborately-decorated vessel belongs to the so-called Alhambra vases produced in Malaga in the late AH 7th–8th / AD 13th–14th century. While its form recalls large storage jars, its monumental size, delicate handles, and lack of structural reinforcements suggest a primarily decorative function. The *khamsa* symbol and *tree of life* design may symbolise protection or royal authority.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/4fd.contextual_description: The term *divan* refers to both a collection of poetry and the literary gatherings of poets, intellectuals and political figures, often held in rulers’ courts or wealthy patrons’ homes, featuring poetry, music and philosophical debates.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/985.contextual_description: In the *Shahnameh*, the account of the Sassanid Emperor Anushirvan, or Khosrow I (reigned 531–579 AD), highlights his wisdom, justice and cultural celebrations. His reign is seen as the golden age of the Sassanid Empire, marked by feasting, artistic performances and intellectual gatherings. The court served as a venue not just for political and military discussions but also for showcasing the emperor’s intelligence and righteousness through grand feasts.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/fe8.contextual_description: This is the largest completely preserved private house in Damascus: it occupies more than 5,500 square meters. In typical Damascene domestic architectural style, the outer appearance is simple but the interior is splendid. It includes an official or formal “male” space and a private or familial “female” space, each provided with a courtyard of flower gardens, fountains and reception rooms decorated with *ablaq* masonry, stone paste patterns and painted wooden panels.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/0b3.contextual_description:
The two miniature paintings from the *Shahnameh* by Firdowsi depict a gathering of courtiers at the royal court. In the *Shahnameh*, the royal court serves as a focus of power and governance because this is the very place the king's powers are exercised as well as represented. The nobles, counsellors, warriors and foreign emissaries all unite in one location to comprise the microcosm of the empire.  
  
Feasts and banquets in the *Shahnameh* mean much more than shared food. They are opportunities for diplomacy, negotiation for honourable alliances and solidifying of ties with others.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/573.contextual_description:
This work features an entertainment scene spanning pages 1b–2a, and on pages 2b–3a; the first section is presented in two facing medallions. It includes 27 miniature scenes illustrating various parables, adorned with *simurg* birds and floral motifs. The chapter headings are illuminated in a period-specific style.  
  
While *Tezkiretü’l Evliya* is primarily a spiritual text, it includes accounts of sufi gatherings where mystics came together for spiritual discussions, poetry and music, blending entertainment with enlightenment.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/f48.contextual_description: This work features ten miniature scenes centred on Timur, depicting battles, meetings and celebrations from the Timurid period. A key event in the *Zafarnāmah* is Timur’s return to Samarkand, celebrated in the Garden of *Bagh-ı Behesht*, symbolising his personal victory and the cultural significance of his reign. The festivities included feasts, music, poetry and gatherings of court and military leaders, highlighting Timur’s achievements and the garden’s representation of political success and prosperity.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/079.contextual_description: This citadel is one of the most important Islamic monuments in Cairo, standing proudly through the ages since its foundation by Salah al-Din (Saladin) on an outcrop of Muqattam Hill to the east of the city. A defensive fortress against the Crusaders, it also served as a residence for the rulers in times of unrest. It continued as such until 1874, when Khedive Isma’il built ‘Abidin Palace to be his seat of rule. The citadel was divided within its walls into a military area and a residential area.

44aa7a89-e3c8-529a-978f-03b6e356816c/d4f.contextual_description: This masterpiece of medieval fortification has been the hallmark of Aleppo since the AH 6th / AD 12th century. Its entrance block alone is an impressive work. Linking the citadel to the city by a stately ramp, it also includes two massively constructed towers which conceal a U-shaped corridor that would force an attacking army to change direction six times, while exposing them to projectiles and burning liquid from gaps in the vaults above. Most of the citadel’s construction, both military as well as the palatial and religious buildings within, date to the Ayyubid al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/96d.contextual_description: One very important aspect of the celebrations during *Surname* was the banquet (*ziyafet*). These grand feasts were not held within palace walls alone; rather, they spread to the streets to include the people in the celebrations. The banquets represented generosity and that the Sultan had the duty of looking after his people. Food distribution to the poor was common. Traditional Ottoman dishes were served in large quantities during the banquets. Gilded tableware and luxurious decorations were used to highlight the grandeur of the event.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/8fb.contextual_description: This miniature painting depicts Zahhak receiving the daughters of Jamshid, Shahrnaz and Arnavaz, who stand before him trembling with fear. Zahhak is seated on his throne, surrounded by courtiers, with a table of golden flasks before him. Attendants on the left carry dishes to present to Zahhak and his guests. The scene captures the etiquette of courtly presentations and the symbolic nature of feasts in the *Shahnameh*, emphasizing themes of hospitality, abundance, and the cultural significance of food in Persian tradition.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/2d1.contextual_description:
The two miniature paintings from the *Shahnameh by Firdowsi* depict a gathering of courtiers at the royal court. In the *Shahnameh*, the royal court serves as a focus of power and governance because this is the very place the king's powers are exercised as well as represented. The nobles, counsellors, warriors and foreign emissaries all cohere in one location to comprise the microcosm of the empire.  
  
Feasts and banquets in the *Shahnameh* mean much more than sharing food. They are opportunities for diplomacy, negotiation for honourable alliances and solidifying ties with others.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/3ea.contextual_description:
Mehrab, accompanied by elephants, musicians and an honour guard, greets Sam and escorts him to Kabul. Waiting for them outside the palace is Mehrab's wife, Sindukht, along with 300 female slaves, each holding a golden cup brimming with gems or musk.  
In her actions, Sindukht upholds the customary Persian hospitality and the way it has been extended towards heroes and leaders. The presents she offers signify her appreciation of Sam and an invitation to his hospitality, showing the respect her family has for him.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/e2a.contextual_description:
Faridun's mother, Faranak, sends him lavish gifts, including Arabian horses, gold, and gems, upon his enthronement. Prominent figures come to pay their respects to the new king. In a painting, Faridun sits on his throne surrounded by courtiers and angels, with his mother’'s gifts displayed before him.  
  
Gift-giving is a central theme in Ferdowsi’s *Shahnameh*, symbolizing more than just material wealth. It reflects values of respect, honour, and social hierarchy, while also reinforcing alliances and driving narratives of heroism and loyalty.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/f4a.contextual_description:
1) Gulnar and Ardashir embrace under the covers, their slippers neatly arranged below. A rope used  
by Gulnar to lower herself from the pavilion roof is tied to a crenelation. Food and flasks of wine  
and water are on the floor.  
2) In the painting, the musician Barbad hides in a cypress tree, enchanting King Khusraw Parviz with his music. The Shah sits on his throne in a garden, enjoying a feast surrounded by courtiers. Nearby, two men hold a quiver of arrows and others carry a torch, indicating the scene takes place at night. A lavish spread of food and drinks is laid out before the Shah, who holds a cup.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/46c.contextual_description:
*The Collection of Ottoman Pictures* is an important album created in the early 19th century illustrating various aspects of Ottoman life, culture and military attire. It includes various sketches that show everyday life and significant events in Ottoman society, with a focus on social gatherings that showcase the complexity and grandeur of the time.  
  
Janissaries often appeared in military settings like training drills, parades and state processions, where they displayed their uniforms and skills.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/14d.contextual_description: The *Mecmua-i Tesavir-i Osmaniye* (*The Collection of Ottoman Pictures*) is a AH 13th / AD 19th century album illustrating Ottoman life and culture. One notable painting shows janissaries, with one playing a musical instrument while others converse around a brazier with cooking food. The collection highlights public festivals, including Bairam celebrations (Eid), featuring feasts, prayers and entertainment, showcasing the empire’s social diversity through various ethnicities and professions.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/7d9.contextual_description:
The miniature portrays a social gathering for entertainment. A servant presents a plate of pomegranates to the person seated on the carpet in the centre. This individual is accompanied by a beautiful young boy who is clapping his hands and reciting a *ghazal* (a type of poem) while musicians provide accompaniment.  
  
In the *Divan-i Hafiz* by Hafiz Shirazi, food and feasting imagery symbolise divine generosity, spiritual fulfilment and the ecstatic union with the divine. Feasts represent spiritual gatherings where seekers share wisdom and love.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/06a.contextual_description: The nilometer, or kiosk of the Nile (*al-Miqyas*), is a significant ancient Egyptian and Islamic architectural structure used to measure the Nile's water levels for agricultural taxes. It resembles a well with three tiers: a circular base, a larger square middle and an even larger top for stability. Water enters through three tunnels with pointed arch openings, the oldest in Islamic Egypt. Inside, a staircase encircles the well, featuring the oldest Arabic inscriptions in Kufic script. A central octagonal marble pillar displays water level measurements.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/03f.contextual_description: The hunting picnic chest is thought to have been a gift from Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria (1830–1916) to Sultan Abdülhamid II. This ornate picnic trunk contains three compartments filled with various items, including plates, flasks, glasses, candlesticks, figurines, forks, knives, penknives, and pipes, all made from metal, glass, and porcelain.

bf8e9642-abed-5b40-9dad-cfc435f0647c/9ca.contextual_description:
A casket designed for transporting food during journeys and campaigns. Later on, a lock was added to protect the contents, as it was common practice to use poison to eliminate political opponents.  
  
This particular casket is made of tin-plated copper and features intricate designs, inscriptions and a medallion adorned with geometric and floral motifs.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/34a.contextual_description:
Enjoyed by the sultans and as an important aspects of royal protocols, coffee was a much valued beverage at the Ottoman court. State officials and ambassadors were welcomed with a cup of coffee served at specific moments of the hospitality protocols depending on the nature of the visit or of the person attending the meeting.  
  
This coffee pot and six matching *zarfs* (cup holders) showcase how the introduction of coffee among the elite and its role in official protocols led to the development of a rich and refined paraphernalia and material culture.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/d80.contextual_description:
The *kahveci başı* was a high official at the Ottoman court in charge of coffee making for the sultans' consumption and for official assemblies. He was at the head of multiple attendants who would help him perform the high standards of his role. This office, introduced during the AH 10th / AD 16th century, underlies the growing importance of coffee and its role in the hospitality protocols of the court.  
  
On this illustration, the *kahveci başı* is recognisable by his posture and embroidered napkin on his shoulder. He is holding a tray covered with a delicate fabric probably covering a coffee set.  
  
Similar protocols were held in the harem where the concubines would endorse the role of the *kahveci başı* and his team.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/190.contextual_description: This vermeil silver bowl with a pedestal foot and hinged lid exemplifies the opulence of Ottoman palace vessels. Decorated with alternating floral patterns and lamb motifs, the bowl incorporates rubies and diamonds set into gold and silver contours. The lid features a chalice design with a cherub base radiating beams. From the late 18th century, Ottoman designs shifted towards Baroque and Rococo styles, as seen in this exquisite example.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/1cf.contextual_description: This exquisite dish, produced at the renowned Yıldız Royal Tile Factory, exemplifies the fusion of artistry and function in objects used within Islamic courts. Designed to serve dried fruits and nuts, its organic, leaflike structure and gilded accents evoke nature's beauty while showcasing the factory's exceptional craftsmanship. Dried fruits and nuts were integral to courtly cuisine, often symbolising hospitality and abundance during royal banquets and celebrations.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/6e4.contextual_description: This small Ottoman silver jug, under 10 centimetres tall, features intricate floral reliefs and partial gilding. Likely influenced by Timurid designs, it reflects the opulent dining customs of the Ottoman elite in the early AH 10 / AD 16th century.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/254.contextual_description: This twelve-sided box, adorned with silver inlay, depicts musicians, revellers and rulers. The cover features interlocking geometric and vegetal designs, while the dome showcases kneeling figures. The intricate craftsmanship underscores the luxury and sophistication of medieval Islamic art.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/484.contextual_description: This Ottoman jug, inspired by Timurid Iran, features dragon-headed handles and scenes of hunting and paradisiacal imagery. The blend of Ottoman, Timurid and European influences showcases the diversity of Islamic art.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/bbf.contextual_description: Produced at the Yıldız Royal Tile Factory – founded in AH 1308 / AH 1891 by Sultan Abdülhamid II – this plate showcases the revival of Turkish tile art. The dark green background is adorned with a gilded *tuğra* (monogram) at its centre and bordered by an intricate gilt edge, reflecting the Factory's blend of traditional craftsmanship and modern Ottoman aesthetics.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/e02.contextual_description: This Samanid bowl from eastern Iran features a Kufic inscription: "Knowledge is the most noble lineage and chivalry the most intricate." The minimalist design, emphasising virtues and prompting conservation, reflects its ceremonial role.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/287.contextual_description: This shallow AH 10th / AD 16th century Ottoman bowl features gilded silver and a rich decoration of arabesque motifs, reflecting the opulence of the sultan's table.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/b80.contextual_description: This hemispherical bowl, with honeycomb faceting and engraved leaves, bears the earliest known *tuğra* (monogram) of Sultan Bayezid II, which served as a control stamp guaranteeing its purity of silver.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/7e8.contextual_description:
This bowl, crafted with vibrant enamel decoration, was a prized possession of medieval Persian courts. Its intricate design, featuring seated figures, cypress trees and kufic script, exemplifies the intersection of art and utility in palatial dining traditions.  
  
Used for serving delicacies during feasts, the bowl's bright colours and delicate craftsmanship reflect the opulence of courtly life. Its calligraphic band adds a layer of sophistication, often conveying blessings or poetry, enhancing the ceremonial atmosphere of royal banquets.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/5bc.contextual_description: This tile plate features cobalt blue, coral red and green slip decoration outlined in black under a transparent glaze. The symmetrical design includes tulips and carnations, with buds and stylised flowers interspersed with cobalt blue Chinese-inspired clouds. A border of white half-rosettes with red centres completed the composition, making it a fine example of Ottoman ceramic art.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/737.contextual_description: This Seljuq period ewer, with its turquoise glaze and epigraphic decoration, is a fine example of how everyday objects were transformed into artistic masterpieces in royal courts. The potters skilfully adopted forms from metalwork, blending functionality with visual appeal.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/5b8.contextual_description: This blue and white bowl, inspired by Chinese porcelain, reflects the global influences on Islamic courtly ceramics. Decorated with stylised flowers and ivy branches, it demonstrates the refinement of ottoman artisans who adapted foreign styles into their own artistic language.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/b69.contextual_description: The tile cup (*tankard*), adorned with tulips and carnations, embodies the Classical Ottoman style of the AH 10th / AD 16th century. Its polychrome decoration and transparent glaze illustrate the artistry of palace workshops. The motifs, rooted in nature, symbolised prosperity and beauty, aligning with the ideals of abundance and refinement that characterised the palatial dining experience.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/021.contextual_description: This fragmentary manuscript of the *Shahnameh* was likely produced for the Shah Abbas the Great after AH 995 / AD 1587. At the bottom, bowls with lids – likely golden or bronze – are arranged, symbolising opulent dining. On the left, a man carries another bowl, while on the right, a smaller figure offers a plate to a third man. All seemingly present food to the central figure, presumably a king, seated on a throne-like platform. This intricate composition exemplifies Persian painting's attention to detail and its ability to narrate grandeur through vivid imagery.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/454.contextual_description:
This particular folio, from the *Shahname* commissioned by Shah Tahmasp I, showcases the tale of Haftvad. The story intertwines Haftvad's destiny with the rise of the Sassanid dynasty.  
  
The lower left of the composition vividly portrays a group of women engaged in what appears to be a cooking activity. This scene aligns with the story's pivotal moment when Haftvad's family, particularly the women, are deceived into inadvertently destroying the magical worm. This moment serves as a cautionary tale, symbolising the fragility of power when dependent on external, mystical forces.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/cee.contextual_description: This dark brown bowl, decorated with white Kufic calligraphy, dates to the AH 4th–5th / AD 10th–11th century. Produced in Nishapur and Afrasiyab, it reflects the region's mastery of ceramic craftsmanship.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/c03.contextual_description: This polychrome underglaze painted dish features a foliated rim and a central medallion surrounded by floral motifs. Combining elements originally designed in court workshops, the pattern includes a wave and rock motif on the rim, inspired by Chinese decorative traditions, illustrating the cross-cultural influences in Islamic art.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/7e3.contextual_description: This hammered brass bowl is richly decorated with gold and silver inlay. Its rim featured lotus and floral motifs, while medallions and cartouches with knotted patterns encircle the body. The geometric design on the base, with a star-shaped interlace and floral elements, is a hallmark of the Mosul school. Likely crafted by a Mosul artisan, it bears inscriptions honouring the Mamluk Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf Qaitbay, wishing him victory and blessings.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/e6f.contextual_description: Located in the heart of Fatimid Cairo, Khan al-Khalili is one of Egypt's oldest and most renowned markets. This bazaar was not only a centre of trade but also a pivotal site of culinary exchange that enriched the courts of the Islamic world. Merchants and traders from across the empire supplied spices, dried fruits, aromatic herbs and rare ingredients essential for crafting the refined dishes served at royal tables. The bustling market connected court kitchens to a vast network of resources, transforming local cuisine into a tapestry of global flavours.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/3bf.contextual_description: This *lahri*, constructed during the reign of Sultan Mulay Isma'il in the AH 11th / AD 17th century, exemplifies the strategic importance of food storage for palace life and governance. This monumental grain silo, built near the royal palace in Meknès, served as a vital reserve for wheat and fodder, ensuring the sustenance of the court, royal stables and surrounding towns during times of conflict, drought or siege.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/18d.contextual_description: This coin, inscribed with the name of the Abbasid caliph and the ruler of Egypt Ahmad ibn Tulun, respectively, is a powerful symbol of sovereignty and economic authority in Islamic courts.

2d56f50e-20ad-5149-ad19-f3994d865877/26a.contextual_description: This Mamluk ceramic dish, gilded and intricately decorated, bears the emblem of the *saqi* (royal cupbearer), highlighting its association with ceremonial dining.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/7d9.contextual_description: This scene encapsulates the profound significance of communal dining in the Islamic world, illustrating how food serves as a central element in social and spiritual gatherings. Within this context, the pomegranate emerges as a powerful symbol: revered in Islamic culture, it represents paradise and the abundance of divine blessings. The prophet recommends consuming pomegranates for their medicinal benefits. Sharing a pomegranate, as seen in this miniature, is also a symbol of sharing good health.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/5a9.contextual_description: This mould is a symbol of sacrifice in Islamic food traditions. It is likely used to form bread or cake for children and carries layers of symbolic meaning in Islamic culture. In Islamic tradition, the ram holds a deep significance, directly tied to the story of the Prophet Abraham and his devotion to Allah. The ram mould underscores food’s role as a medium for social, cultural and spiritual expression in Islam. It also represents the act of sacrificing an animal for a guest or a visitor.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/8f2.contextual_description: Decorated with a palm tree motif, the *magharif* embodies the cultural and spiritual importance of the date palm in Oman and the broader Islamic world. Dates are often consumed to break the fast during the holy month of Ramadan and reflect sustenance, sharing and hospitality in Islamic tradition. This spoon, therefore, is not a simple tool; it is a cultural artifact that conveys the deep-rooted symbolism of the date palm as a source of life, sustenance and cultural identity across the Islamic world.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/619.contextual_description: Wheat and olive branches depicted in this relief carry profound significance in parts of the Islamic world. Wheat, believed to have originated in the Fertile Crescent, shaped the region's dietary traditions, making bread a staple food across the Muslim world. The olive tree, blessed in Islam and central to many countries in Bilad al-Sham, symbolises a deep connection to the land, reflecting resilience, sustenance and spiritual significance in the region's culture and traditions.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/d38.contextual_description: The Surah al-Anbiya states, “We made from water every living thing“ (Quran 21:30). In Islam, water is seen as a sacred blessing necessary for life and purity. The intricate decorations of these bottles reflect a reverence for water as a sacred gift from Allah and call on believers to remember their gratitude and patronage. The intricate decoration present on these bottles reflects the ritual importance of water: it is a source of both physical sustenance and spiritual purity, essential for ablution.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/5fe.contextual_description: This ewer is noteworthy in that it can be closed to protect water from spilling or evaporating, highlighting the preciousness of water in the Islamic world.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/b46.contextual_description: In the Islamic world, coffee embodies a central social and cultural role. During significant celebrations such as Eid, coffee is a prominent feature in the Turkish and broader Islamic social calendar. It serves as a gesture of goodwill and a bridge between family, friends and community members. Nowadays, coffee is the first drink offered to guests in Islamic society, representing an act of hospitality and generosity.

6a5071c2-d01d-519b-9fc3-c51994784f7e/57e.contextual_description: Dates, a staple food in the region, hold profound significance not only as a source of nourishment but also as a symbol of amity and welcome. Their inclusion in this collection emphasises the social norms surrounding the reception of guests and the rituals that accompany such gatherings. It symbolises sustenance, generosity and the connection to the land. Offering dates to guests signifies respect and goodwill, reinforcing the bonds of community and friendship.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/03e.contextual_description: During the Mamluk period in Cairo, hexagonal tables made from wood or metal became common household items. These tables played an essential role in daily life, keeping food or other items elevated from the floor. More than just practical furniture, they symbolised the heart of hospitality, where meals were shared in a communal and welcoming manner. Alongside the other related elements, they set the stage for the intimate act of dining together, an essential part of receiving guests and fostering bonds.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/40c.contextual_description: This piece represents the act of gathering of dishes, plates and cup to be shared on a table to eat.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/838.contextual_description: Because food is eaten with the hands in Arab and Persian custom, hosts would frequently offer to pour water from this vessel into a guest’s hands in a washing ceremony.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/d2d.contextual_description: This pot is used to prepare food for the household and for guests inside the kitchen before being put in plates, on the tray and then on the table.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/6a6.contextual_description: Samanid ceramics, known for their refined craftsmanship, often bear inscriptions that inspire conversation or offer blessings. This bowl, with its thoughtful inscription, reflects a deep appreciation for the intellectual and moral values of the time, likely serving not just as a functional object but as a symbolic piece that highlighted the ideals of wisdom and noble conduct during shared meals and gatherings. This group of objects reflects artifacts used in private settings to impress guests and elevate the dining experience.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/646.contextual_description: Everyday life in Oman is infused with the mingled scents of flowers, aromatic woods, resins, spices and herbs. Incense has long had a place in Omani society; burners may be carried from room to room, passed beneath clothing to envelop the wearer in a cloud of perfume or positioned under a pyramidal fumigator made from split date palm ribs. This incense burner is also used when receiving a guest in the house in order to create a more pleasant atmosphere.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/2ce.contextual_description: This carpet exemplifies a long-standing tradition in the Islamic world of sitting on the floor to share meals, engage in conversation and partake in music and dance. The *majlis*, a private social gathering space, often centre around a carpet like this, which provides a warm and inviting environment for communal activities. The practice of sitting on the floor to eat symbolises hospitality and humility, reflecting a sense of equality among guests and hosts, warmth and mutual respect.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/754.contextual_description: This residential winter reception chamber (*qa'a*) exemplifies the refined social traditions of the late Ottoman period. In affluent households like this one, the reception chamber was meticulously maintained, with updates made over time to reflect changing styles and trends. These reception chambers were not only spaces of luxury but also venues for expressing community, generosity and the essential tradition of gathering around meals to connect with others.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/d84.contextual_description: This tent symbolises the act of gathering under one roof, embodying the essence of community and hospitality. Much like the traditional Persian *iwan*, which serves as a bridge between indoor and outdoor spaces, the tent provides an intimate and shaded area for people to come together; it is a deeply social and spiritual act that fosters unity and connection. The tent’s structure not only offers a space for physical shelter but also represents the symbolic shelter of coming together in harmony.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/a91.contextual_description: The artist beautifully captures the communal act of serving and sharing food. Such imagery highlights the significance of food as a social and ceremonial practice, often associated with hospitality and celebration. The portrayal of communal dining underscores the importance of food as a connector in both courtly and everyday life, making it a central theme in this collection. This specific scene represents the social gathering of Yusuf, Zulaikha and their friends in an intimate setting.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/4fd.contextual_description: The *Divan* illustrates an important aspect of traditional social gatherings in the Islamic world. These gatherings often involved communal entertainment such as poetry recitations, music and storytelling in a private gathering, all in a context where food and drink played a central role. The *Divan* reflects the cultural and intellectual exchanges during these gatherings, as well as the emphasis on conviviality through shared food, drink and the pleasure of company.

2d0d49ee-aadb-57d5-a311-4e85d98f1dc1/dab.contextual_description: One of the scenes in this illustrated poem depicts the gathering of two lovers with cups next to them. This serene moment represents not just a romantic connection but also the spiritual act of hospitality and nourishment. Eating together in a lush, tranquil setting reflects the cultural ideals of generosity, togetherness and love, transforming food into a medium of emotional and spiritual unity, deeply rooted in the Islamic tradition of communal harmony.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/be9.contextual_description: The prophet said, “The best form of charity is to give someone water“. The fountain, an element commonly found in the Islamic world, highlights the importance of sharing water. It represents a symbol of charity and civic bond. The upper section is adorned with an engraved marble panel featuring two lines of Diwani Arabic inscriptions. The inscription honours the fountain’s builders, offering gratitude for their contribution, reflecting the high regard for public service and charitable acts in Islam.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/6f6.contextual_description: In this case, the *sabil* is a part of the madrasa or the Qur'anic school, used to share water with the students of Islam.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/2c3.contextual_description: Benefactors were responsible for the creation of these fountains. Attached to each one, on a plaque of marble or shale, in Arabic or Ottoman Turkish, is an inscription extolling the merits of the benefactor.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/2ba.contextual_description: This reservoir served as a central gathering point for the residents of the Umayyad citadel. This structure symbolises the vital role of water in Islam as a unifying force that brings the community together.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/14f.contextual_description: This complex stands as a symbol of Ottoman commitment to public welfare, embodying the Islamic ideals of charity and social responsibility. Covering 22,000 square meters, this expansive complex was meticulously designed not only for worship but also as a sanctuary for learning, health and social services. Key elements include the mosque, guesthouses, a madrasa for education, a hospital for healing, an imaret (soup kitchen) dedicated to feeding the poor and essential storerooms.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/50b.contextual_description: This monument is a remarkable example of Mamluk architectural and cultural priorities, specifically designed as a refuge and communal residence for Sufi mystics. With its 100 cells spread over three floors, the Khanqah offered dedicated space for personal devotion, meditation and scholarly pursuits. The Khanqah was thus both a spiritual and social space where communal meals reinforced the bonds among residents, symbolising a collective commitment to simplicity, generosity and shared purpose.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/b26.contextual_description: This imaret stands as a remarkable example of food symbolism through charitable practice in the Islamic world. Built by Sultan Murad I in honor of his mother, Nilüfer Hatun, this structure not only serves as an architectural testament to her memory but also as a charitable institution or imaret, reflecting the Islamic values of generosity and care for the poor. Imarets, common in Ottoman architecture, provided free meals to the needy and travellers, a symbolic gesture of communal support and spiritual duty.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/c18.contextual_description: The Takiyya served as a place that provided accommodation and free meals to pilgrims, emphasising Islam's commitment to hospitality and charity. This monument highlights the importance Islam places on helping the poor and needy by offering them food, which is seen as a fundamental act of generosity and compassion. The provision of food reflects the deeply ingrained value of sharing in Islamic culture, where feeding others is not only a sign of hospitality but also a way of fulfilling religious duties of charity and care for the less fortunate.

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/831.contextual_description: This complex reflects the profound importance of food sharing in Islamic culture. This multifunctional complex includes a large kitchen, two ovens, two bakeries, a *sabil*, a large *khan* (inn), a mosque and a Sufi *ribat* (hospice). Each day, over 1000 meals were provided to the needy and visitors, regardless of their identity or religion, a tradition that mirrors the operations of the *zawiya* (Sufi teaching centre) and the *arbita* (Sufi hospice).

efb15863-4613-54f9-9175-ff58c521d782/5b6.contextual_description: This pot would collect and measure the alms given as charity by the people of Medina in Saudi Arabia. The cylindrical jar features the *basmala* or Muslim invocation and Qur'anic verses in *thuluth* and *naskh* script. This container was used to gather the alms or the money for the poor. With *zakat* (charity) as one of the pillars of Islam, wealthy Muslims are obligated to donate alms. It shows how giving to the less fortunate is a part of connecting the Islamic community by sharing money and food.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/088.contextual_description: In rural northeast Syria, communal feasts are essential during major celebrations. These gatherings bring families and friends together, with the ritual of slaughtering sheep to mark the occasion. The meal itself is a communal experience, with small groups sitting in a circle on the floor. This practice, rooted in the traditions of nomadic societies that began settling in the late 19th century AD, embodies the core values of food sharing in Islamic culture, reinforcing solidarity, community bonds and hospitality.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/d6b.contextual_description: During large festivals and big feasts, Bedouin women gather to cook vast amounts of food in open fireplaces, typically set up under tent roofs specifically raised for the occasion.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/ed6.contextual_description: Home-made traditional bread is also prepared and shared during everyday life as well as feasts.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/892.contextual_description: Home-made traditional bread is also prepared and shared during important occasions and feasts.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/7da.contextual_description: These guesthouses (known as *madafa* or *oda*) were social hubs where village men would gather to discuss matters, share stories, exchange news and share a meal or a drink. Managed by a *mukhtar* (village headman) or *shaykh* (tribal leader), the guesthouse symbolised the village’s hospitality and community spirit. Though guesthouses are no longer as commonly used, they remain a symbol of the deep-rooted customs of sharing spaces in rural environments.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/411.contextual_description: In these meetings in the guest house, there is an offering of bitter coffee (*qahwa murra*), a timeless gesture of hospitality in traditional Arab culture, particularly in the Levant and the Arabian Peninsula.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/15e.contextual_description: Only very wealthy tribal leaders or village headmen could employ a coffee cook (*qahwaji*) responsible for making the bitter coffee and serving it.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/2f4.contextual_description: The miniature scene depicts a “servant” presenting food to his “master,” reflecting social hierarchies and hospitality customs integral to nomadic life in the Islamic world. These theatrical miniatures not only entertained but also conveyed European perspectives on Middle Eastern traditions, sometimes romanticising or exoticising these interactions. Through scenes like this, audiences were exposed to cultural elements such as food-sharing practices, adding a layer of fascination with the distant lands and rituals depicted.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/5c0.contextual_description: This settlement reflects the Khawarij's unique approach to sustaining life in a nomadic landscape, balancing the need for a settled, stable source of food and water with the surrounding arid conditions. This enduring settlement highlights the symbiosis between architecture, environmental adaptation and communal life in the Islamic world, illustrating how nomadic traditions were transformed to support sustainable urban communities in the heart of the desert.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/f50.contextual_description: In the Islamic world, coffee houses were vibrant social spaces where life’s rituals of conversation, connection and hospitality were enacted in an urban environment. This setting captures the essence of social gatherings that revolve around shared food and drink. Traditional coffee houses offered much more than refreshments: they were urban hubs of social exchange that took place in the heart of the city where men met to sip coffee, enjoy sweet or savoury dishes and smoke water pipes, known as *narghile*.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/38a.contextual_description: Coffee houses are a big part of the urbanised Islamic world; this one is in Turkey.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/2df.contextual_description: This shows another example of a coffee house in the Islamic world, in this case in Tunisia.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/7c7.contextual_description: This illustration portrays Muslim societies transitioning from traditional Bedouin lifestyles to urbanised living. From the perspective of the French coloniser, this shift symbolises the supposed "progress" brought by colonisation, contrasting the communal, urban atmosphere with the simplicity of nomadic life. This visual serves as a tool to highlight colonial views on modernisation and urban development, emphasising the coloniser's role in reshaping the social and cultural dynamics of Muslim Arab communities.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/e6f.contextual_description: The *khan* is an essential part of the Muslim city or *medina*. It is not only a *suq* to sell goods, but also serves as a meeting place in the city; people gather around a coffee or a meal to share a communal space inside the urban environment. The act of dining and conversing in these public spaces reflects the deep-rooted values of alimentary conviviality and community that underscore daily life in an urban environment.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/64c.contextual_description: It is said that the tradition of *suhur* has originated in the streets of Cairo in the ninth century. This practice of waking people up to have a small meal before fasting wouldn’t have been possible in a rural setting. The concept of *suhur* revolves around a shared urbanised community structure of people where the *msaharati* would walk the streets of the city to wake people up. Such a system relied on the dense population and collective organisation found in cities.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/336.contextual_description: In tribal societies, the generosity of influential tribal chiefs is often demonstrated by the preparation and serving of vast amounts of food during significant events or celebrations. Food was customarily presented on enormous trays. In contrast to the individual plate that was introduced in the urbanised areas that emphasise personal space, individualism and formalised dining habits found in urban areas, this practice symbolises equality, trust, a strong sense of community and the deep bonds of hospitality central to the Bedouin culture.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/dba.contextual_description: Similar to the huge tray, these big plates are used in a traditional Moroccan setting where food is shared from a common plate.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/0e7.contextual_description: Similar to the huge tray, these big plates are used in a traditional Moroccan setting where food is shared from a common plate.

39cb0400-0972-5deb-b20b-7ff5ae2ab902/175.contextual_description: Similar to the huge tray, these big plates are used in a traditional Tunisian setting where food is shared from a common plate.

88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3/16a.contextual_description: The Qur’an states in verses 2:173, 6:118, and 6:138 that the name of Allah must be mentioned when slaughtering an animal, otherwise the meat is not considered halal for a Muslim. This painting is directly related to this Islamic rule, as the sheikh is instructing his disciples to refrain from accepting meat that they do not know.

88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3/b9d.contextual_description: As stated in *hadith* sources such as Tirmizi, Bukhari, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hajar, and Ibn Hanbal, the Prophet Muhammad placed significant emphasis on the importance of offering food, sharing meals, and treating guests with hospitality. In this picture the Prophet Abraham requests that an old pagan priest convert to Islam so that he may offer him a meal. However, a voice from the heavens indicates that it is not appropriate to send an old man away from the table hungry. This illustrates the significance of sharing food in Islam regardless of religious affiliation.

88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3/a2a.contextual_description: There are multiple verses in the Qur’an that advise avoidance of alcohol. For instance, Surah Maide (5:90) prohibits Muslims from consuming alcohol. However, it should be noted that not all Muslims adhere to this prohibition, and alcohol consumption is prevalent among Muslims. This work reflects the prohibition and shows that Islamic dietary rules are not always strictly followed.

88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3/555.contextual_description: The bowl, inscribed with the Surahs *Ikhlas* and *Felak*, may have been used in the hope of achieving healing and protection through the power of the verses inscribed upon it. It is considered an important artefact for the exhibition, as it exemplifies the interconnection between religion and food.

88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3/d85.contextual_description: The consumption of food and drink from bowls containing verses from the Qur’an, the most beautiful names of Allah, or religious and talismanic phrases, was believed to counter the effects of poisons, fevers, and other physical ailments. This practice is closely linked to religion, medicine, and astrology.

88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3/0f8.contextual_description: The consumption of food and drink from bowls containing verses from the Qur’an, the most beautiful names of Allah, or religious and talismanic phrases, was believed to counter the effects of poisons, fevers, and other physical ailments. 88243574-b43d-52e0-96f3-587fec892cd3/83b.contextual_description: The practice of washing one’s hands before and after eating is a Sunnah, or tradition, of Prophet Muhammad, as evidenced by sources such as Muslim, Bukhari, and Tirmizi. This meticulously crafted and refined item is linked to that *hadith*.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/b03.contextual_description: Coffee is important in hospitality in Turkish and Islamic cultures, especially during holidays, when families come together, and guests are served traditional drinks.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/009.contextual_description: In the Islamic culture of the Middle East, offering coffee to visitors during Eids is a significant tradition that has endured for centuries. This item represents that tradition.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/2c6.contextual_description: In the Islamic culture of the Middle East, offering coffee to visitors during Eids is a significant tradition that has endured for centuries. This pot is a tool used in the making of Arabic coffee.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/d4c.contextual_description: The item is part of coffee culture. Turkish coffee is a symbol of hospitality that conveys respect and welcome. Ornate serving items, such as cup stands, reflect the care shown to the valued guest.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/fac.contextual_description: In the Islamic culture of the Middle East, offering coffee to visitors during Eids is a significant tradition that has endured for centuries. These traditional coffee coolers were used after the coffee was roasted. This item is also an important artefact of the preparation phase.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/a69.contextual_description: Coffee is important for hospitality in Turkish and Islamic culture, especially during holidays such as festivals, when families come together and guests are served traditional drinks. The pot’s beautiful design highlights its use in these special preparations, connecting it to the theme of religious celebrations and hospitality.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/5b6.contextual_description: This bronze pot, used for collecting alms, belongs to the theme of religious celebrations and rituals of giving. During these festivals, the act of *zakat*, a core pillar of Islam, reflects the spirit of community, purification, and blessings, in which the wealthy share their surplus with those in need.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/b58.contextual_description: *Hag al Layla*, celebrated in the UAE and other GCC countries on the 15th of Sha’ban, symbolises the welcome of the holy month of Ramadan. During the celebrations children visit neighbours and are offered sweets. A similar tradition is observed in Türkiye on a similar holiday. Its purpose is to delight children with sweets and to strengthen the bonds of neighbourliness and community through sharing food.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/1dd.contextual_description: The tradition of offering sweets to guests during festivals is common in Türkiye and reflects hospitality and celebration. This item highlights that tradition, evidence of the respect held for guests and the joy of sharing during festivals.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/a00.contextual_description: The tradition of offering sweets to guests during festivals is common in Türkiye and reflects hospitality and celebration. This item highlights that tradition, evidence of the respect held for guests and the joy of sharing during festivals.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/3a4.contextual_description: The *Karagöz* and *Hacivat* shadow play has been a key feature of Ottoman and Turkish traditional entertainment, especially during religious festivals such as Ramadan. Performed by a single artist, this form of shadow play represents the diversity of Ottoman society and serves as a reflection of its multi-ethnic makeup. Its inclusion under the “Religious Festivals, Preparation, and Dishes” theme highlights its cultural significance as a form of storytelling and entertainment during occasions that foster communal gatherings and celebration.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/64c.contextual_description: In the Middle East the tradition of beating drums during Ramadan has been observed for centuries to wake people in order to eat (*suhur*) before sunrise. This item derives from that tradition.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/545.contextual_description: This mosque is especially important during religious festivals, as visiting mosques for prayer and reflection is a key tradition in Islamic culture. It is a historically significant gathering place for worship during major Islamic holidays like Eid and Ramadan, reflecting the theme of preparation for religious observance.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/310.contextual_description: On the tenth day of the month of Muharram in Türkiye, both Sunni and Alevi-Bektashi Muslims engage in the preparation and sharing of *ashura* (also known as Noah’s Pudding), a ritual dish believed to symbolise prosperity. The black cauldron, which represents the ritual of making *ashura*, occupies a particularly significant position within Bektashi culture.

d8c7a0b9-0782-5614-b08e-7125add26515/0e2.contextual_description: In Islamic culture, rose water is served to guests, particularly in Türkiye, on occasions such as the anniversary of the birth of the Prophet Muhammad (Mevlid) and religious holidays. Consequently, rose water bottles, which are crafted in accordance with the social status of the owner and are intended to impress guests, hold a significant position in Islamic culture.

cacd508c-ac3e-57b1-bbbe-26babcbf2131/4b2.contextual_description: The “Sufi Assembly” miniature, created in the early AH 11th / 17th century, depicts a nocturnal gathering of dervishes. The scene, enriched with Persian verses, reflects key Sufi themes of spiritual renunciation and introspection. Through its serene imagery and calligraphy, the work conveys the Sufi path of inner purification and the search for deeper truths.

cacd508c-ac3e-57b1-bbbe-26babcbf2131/3cd.contextual_description: The kitchen serves as the primary location for evaluating the suitability of individuals seeking to become Mevlevi disciples and for training accepted disciples. The reproduction in Konya, home of Mevlevism, currently known as the Konya Mevlana Museum, illustrates Mevlevi training and table culture. Those who wish to join the order must spend the first few days observing in the kitchen, in the *saka postu* shown in the picture.

c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8/8b9.contextual_description: The archaeological site of Tall Abu Sarbut in the Jordan Valley reveals the intricate relationship among agriculture, economy, and environment during the Mamluk period (AH 648–923 / AD 1250–1517). As a key storage and distribution centre, the site played a pivotal role in the regional sugar industry, which relied on the fertile lands of the valley for sugarcane cultivation. This was one of several sites associated with sugar production in the Levant, renowned for the superior quality of its sugar, which drove significant demand from European markets.

c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8/231.contextual_description: The foggaras are an ingenious water distribution and irrigation system developed in the arid Saharan regions, notably in Gourara and Touat. Dating back to ancient times, they exemplify human creativity in overcoming harsh environmental challenges. By drilling tunnels at mountain bases to access underground water reservoirs, the foggaras channel water to the surface, sustaining agriculture in oases. The comb-like distribution structures ensure efficient water use, sustaining food production in extreme conditions.

c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8/cd3.contextual_description: This dagger belonged to Imam Saif bin Sultan (r. AH 1104–23 / AD 1692–1711), a ruler from the Yaruba dynasty in Oman. During his reign he made significant contributions to Oman’s political, cultural, and economic development. He improved water use with *aflaj* systems, expanded the cultivation of crops like wheat, barley, and sugarcane, and planted date palms and fruit trees. He also introduced new plants such as turmeric, saffron, and coffee, and promoted beekeeping to support agriculture.

c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8/bc5.contextual_description:
Sultan Mulay Isma‘il (r. AH 1083–1140 / AD 1672–1727) ensured a reliable water supply not only for the residents of the kasbah and public baths, but also for the lush gardens and orchards surrounding the town, which provided fresh fruits and vegetables daily. To achieve this he commissioned the construction of an artificial lake.  
The lake was fed by a sophisticated water management system: ten wells, dug near the Sahrij below the silo, channeled water into the lake through *norias* and a network of ceramic conduits. Additionally, fresh water from the Wadi Bufekrane supplemented this supply.

c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8/47e.contextual_description:
*Norias* stand as a testament to remarkable engineering. While their origins date back to ancient times, the medieval period witnessed a notable increase in references to them in Islamic geographical writings, highlighting their improved designs and widespread adoption.  
Designed to lift water into aqueducts, *norias* played a crucial role in irrigation and the supply of potable water. Constructed primarily from poplar wood and supported by stone aqueducts and dams, they required regular maintenance to function effectively. At their peak, the city of Hama featured up to fifty *norias*.

c409179d-f3e3-5b3c-b6d6-f525504051a8/a55.contextual_description:
The development of irrigation and hydraulic systems in Al-Andalus enabled the introduction of new plant species, the expansion of arable land and a more diverse diet. It changed working methods, the agricultural cycle and the landscape.
