fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/d80.contextual_description: The Manises ceramics industry gradually developed its own style, producing a wide range of characteristic typologies and iconographic motifs. The variety of coats of arms found on them is evidence of the taste of the Christian elite for this style of tableware.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/e50.contextual_description: The 19th century saw strong enthusiasm for the Islamic arts of Al-Andalus. This led to the revival of Nasrid-Mudéjar style, inspiring artists and invigorating the ceramics industry of Manises. The Valencia factory responded by reproducing Mudéjar-like artefacts such as this plate.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/402.contextual_description:
High-quality blue and white Chinese porcelain from Jingdezhen became very popular among the elite of the Middle East around the AH 8th / AD 14th century. The products exported were designed to appeal to Islamic visual tastes, and their shapes were adapted to be perfect recipients for traditional Islamic dishes.  
  
This plate was found in Mamluk, Syria, and dates from the AH 8th / AD 14th century.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/5b8.contextual_description:
During the AH 9th / AD 15th century, the demand for blue and white porcelain was so strong that many Middle Eastern local production centres started copying the same decorative scheme.  
  
Some ceramics scrupulously imitated the Chinese style, such as this Iznik (Ottoman) bowl, highly influenced by Chinese designs, such as peonies and the so-called “Chinese clouds".

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/cce.contextual_description:
Other centres, inspired by the blue and white contrast of Chinese ceramics, specialised in defining a new visual identity, mixing the contrasting visual appeal of the blue and white porcelain with their own iconography.  
  
This plate, for example, probably made in Kirman (Iran), depicts tigers and birds freely displayed in a thick vegetations.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/555.contextual_description:
The appropriation of blue and white porcelain motifs by the Islamic potters did not stop the importation of Chinese wares. This bowl was produced in China for the Ottoman market. It was probably part of a large tableware set custom-made for important individuals and likely dispersed today into public and private collections.  
  
It might have matched a similar large tureen, whose shape could originally have been created for the European market before it became attractive to the Islamic one.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/b2b.contextual_description:
This type of vivid coloured porcelain belongs to a figurative style named “Famille Rose” or “Rose Canton”. The style was very popular among Islamic elites, who ordered them custom-made, as the central medallion inscription exemplifies. They were probably among the most expensive luxury items, as the production process was more complex and longer than for blue and white examples.  
  
A similar plate displaying the same inscription but a different design was sold at auction in 2024, which indicates that they could have been part of a large set.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/fb6.contextual_description: This life-sized oil painting from the Zand period probably once hung in a niche in a reception hall. It shows an idealised portrait of the elite lifestyle, mirroring the pomp typical of such an environment. Staring directly at the viewer, the courtier holds an engraved wine glass that matches a square decanter typical of European imports of the time. By her side is a bowl (possibly of the “Famille Rose” type) filled with pomegranates on a matching plate.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/9a1.contextual_description:
At around the same time as in Persia, Mughal India was importing square bottles similar to this one, whose shape derived from the wooden chests in which they were transported.  
  
The preserved Mughal examples are lavishly decorated with vegetal or figurative motifs, probably painted locally after their importation.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/e28.contextual_description:
These three decanters are ornamented with a portrait of the Qajar sultan Naser-al-Din Shah. Produced by the Bohemian (now Czech Republic) glass industry, which boomed during the AH 13th / AD 19th century, they are examples of exported glassware produced in Europe to suit the taste of the Qajar elite. Such pieces contributed to the visual propaganda of the dynasty, and would have fitted perfectly into their collections of foreign tableware.  
  
This type of glassware was probably produced during the second half of the 19th century before going out of fashion and/or decreasing in quality.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/1d5.contextual_description:
Artefacts such as this ewer and tray combine Northern European-style metalwork with a Renaissance version of Mamluk motifs. The style was initially called “Veneto-Saracenic” in reference to its probable manufacture in Venice by Muslim craftsmen. Such artefacts are considered today more likely to have been created by Mamluks for export, to be sent to Egypt or Syria for decoration, or to be European copies.  
  
Regardless of its origin, this set is evidence of a tableware industry inspired by the Near East to suit important European families during the AH 9th / AD 15th and AH 10th / AD 16th centuries.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/a7c.contextual_description:
During the AH 8th / AD 14th and AH 9th / AD 15th centuries, Mamluk metalworkers developed a range of wares specifically to appeal to European tastes and markets. Coats of arms appeared on many pieces.  
  
This box is thought to have held expensive spices conveyed to the West.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/a69.contextual_description: This silver-plated copper coffee pot reflects European Baroque influence on Ottoman decorative arts, notably in its ornate design and curving shape. While most coffee pots were made from inexpensive materials, luxurious versions like this one were crafted for affluent households to serve esteemed guests. The Ottoman Baroque style, blending European motifs with traditional forms, emerged in the 1740s and remained popular until the 1820s, when newer European designs gained prominence.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/190.contextual_description: This lidded bowl is one example of luxurious Ottoman-era vessels. Made of vermeil silver, it features a floral pattern and hanging lamp motifs. The vessel, influenced by Western Baroque and Rococo styles of the late 18th century, departs from classical Ottoman designs. Its body is adorned with rubies and diamonds, while the lid is decorated by a chalice supported by a cherubic foot with emanating rays. The design reflects Ottoman craftsmanship and the influence of European artistic trends.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/fbd.contextual_description: Kütahya emerged as a prominent Ottoman ceramic centre in the late 17th century, earning the nickname “The Sèvres of the East” due to its intricate and exotic designs that were admired by Europeans. This egg-shaped ewer, a rare example of AH 12th / AD 18th century Kütahya ware, showcases the fusion of Eastern and Western artistic influences. It can be attributed to the town’s Armenian community, which played a significant role in ceramic production. Decorated with cobalt brushstrokes on a white background, it exemplifies the craftsmanship of the period.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/456.contextual_description: Branko Šotra (1906–1960) created carved wooden ensembles of peškuns (stools) in the 1930s, blending traditional Oriental forms with Art Deco style. These decorated tables and chairs, popular in Belgrade’s Bosnian rooms, featured scenes of rural life and geometric motifs.

fbc88500-65ce-5081-90df-faf94cdf1a32/6e3.contextual_description: In AH 1329 / AD 1911, following the Ottoman departure from Tripoli, Binjamin Uziyel, a consulate official, conducted research on establishing sugar factories in Turkey after a visit to Genoa. He prepared a comprehensive report for the Istanbul chamber of commerce detailing the feasibility of setting up sugar factories and exploring the utilisation of sugar beets in Turkey.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/603.contextual_description: According to the current state of research, Jewish populations have lived in North Africa (more precisely in today’s Tunisia) since the Punic period. This watercolour representing a Jewish household highlights the cultural similarities between the Jewish and Muslim communities of this region. The architecture and decor of the dwelling reveal a similar way of living, and the clothing shows a similar way of dressing. The commonalities extended to other spheres, including food preparation, and recipes remain a noteworthy shared cultural feature.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/a3f.contextual_description:
Wells are meeting places for locals and people from far and wide, a place to find refreshment, get acquainted, talk, exchange opinions and experiences about life and food, even about cooking. Water connects everyone; it is essential for life.  
  
Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda’s well (*sabil*) is a fine example of coexistence through water use. Built during the Ottoman Turkish occupation by Commander ‘Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda ibn Husayn Jawish al-Qardughliand, its style, form and decoration show the interaction of several cultures, resulting in a blend of Mamluk and Ottoman-Turkish artistic styles.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/1a2.contextual_description: Among other Judeo-North African dishes is the *t’fina pkaila*, a spinach (in Arabic *pkaila*) sauce that can be eaten with couscous; *nikituches*, very small semolina balls eaten with sauce and called *berkukes* in its Algerian version; *matbucha* and *slata mechuia*, both Berber salads made from roasted peppers, tomatoes, garlic and/or onions; various forms of couscous, and harissa, a traditional North African spicy condiment, among others.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/8a1.contextual_description: What dish could be more British than fish and chips? The earliest record of the sale of fish and chips by Jewish traders in the streets of London dates to the early 19th century, and a recipe for it appeared in the first Jewish cookbook in English (1846). However, research has shown that the very first record of the recipe can be traced back to the AH 7th / AD 13th century cookbook by al-Tujībī, an exiled and nostalgic chronicler from Al-Andalus who recorded the dishes of his homeland and North Africa. His fish and chips recipe specifies the use of vinegar as a condiment, just like in the current British tradition.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/029.contextual_description:
Couscous is a famous Berber dish introduced to Al-Andalus during the AH 6th / AD 12th century during the occupation of the Iberian Peninsula by the Marrakesh Almohad dynasty. From there it spread to Syria and the rest of the Islamic world. But it did not charm only the East, as a recipe for a couscous dish to be served at the king’s table appeared in a cookbook of the Spanish King Philip II.  
  
The appreciation for couscous among Spanish Christians is also evident in the couscous tableware and utensils produced by the ceramics industry of Manises.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/d25.contextual_description:
This type of ceramic jar was used to store olive oil. During the Spanish Inquisition, Muslims and Jews were forced to convert to Christianity. Their cooking habits, closely linked to their communities’ identities, were targeted by inquisitors in order to force them to prove loyalty to their new religion.  
  
Despite its wide use in Mediterranean cultures, olive oil was virtually forbidden during the Inquisition, to be replaced by pork fat (*tocino*), banned by Muslim and Jewish dietary laws. Such prohibitions also harmed some *andalusi* Christians that shared culinary customs with the oppressed.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/b8a.contextual_description:
Multiple medieval Islamic cookbooks provide us with recipes for special Christian events. Known as *muzawwarāt*, meaning counterfeit, these vegetarian meals were a form of compensatory or alternative dishes for special occasions, such as during Lent or for meat-free day. They were also recommended for the sick.  
  
This bowl was made for the royal court by a Christian potter from Hira. It showcases the long presence of native Christian communities in today’s Iraq.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/0b3.contextual_description:
With every change of power and enduring contact came new food traditions that migrated between local and arriving cultures. This was true even in troubled times, as during the era of the Crusades.  
  
This striking Ayyubid glass canteen is ornamented with mixed Islamic and crusader iconography, testimony to the mutual cultural exchanges of the AH 7th / 13th century in Syria. It exemplifies vividly the porosity of the two cultures that extended to food. For example, an Ayyubid cookbook from the same period provides a recipe for a tasty and slow-cooked Frankish roast.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/6e7.contextual_description: The coffee house is a state within a state, a world of its own where local people, friends and travellers from far and wide meet, read, play board games, listen to music or chat, tell stories, and exchange news or recipes. Coffee, coffee drinking and the café span worlds, connecting relatives and strangers. Today we know that the coffee plant originated in Ethiopia, was first planted in Mecca in the AH 9th / AD 15th century, and then, through the Ottoman Turkish Empire, it began to conquer the world, aided by the Egyptian Mamluk Sultanate.

8818b6b4-68f6-5cce-bc26-8dc0b3603340/b0b.contextual_description: Food markets have always been places where people could find local and imported goods, fresh produce, and prepared meals. Visitors might discover foods from near or far, exchange information, and share recipes. This Orientalist painting represents this space valued for the sharing of culinary culture. It was executed by the Italian Amadeo Preziosi, who documented his travels in paintings, providing a glimpse of the East to 19th century Europeans.
